title: Amines as bases and nucleophiles
keyIdea: An amine is ammonia with one or more hydrogens replaced by carbon groups. Count the carbons bonded directly to N: one is primary, two secondary, three tertiary. The lone pair on N makes amines bases (RNH₂ + H⁺ → RNH₃⁺, an ammonium salt) and nucleophiles. Alkyl groups push electron density onto N, so ethylamine is a stronger base than ammonia; in phenylamine the pair is delocalised into the ring, so it is weaker. Ammonia and a haloalkane give a mixture, because each amine formed is also a nucleophile. A large excess of ammonia favours the primary amine.

kid: An amine is like ammonia, NH₃, with carbon groups in place of some H atoms. To class it, count the carbons joined to the N. One carbon means primary. Two means secondary. Three means tertiary.
Look only at the N. In (CH₃)₃C–NH₂ the N has just one carbon on it, so it is primary. Do not count carbons further out, as you would for an alcohol.

The N has a lone pair of electrons. It can grab an H⁺ from an acid, so amines are bases. Ethylamine and HCl make ethylammonium chloride, CH₃CH₂NH₃⁺ Cl⁻. A spare pair on N makes a stronger base. An ethyl group pushes electrons onto N. In phenylamine the pair spreads into the ring. So phenylamine is weaker than ammonia, and ethylamine is stronger.

The lone pair also lets amines attack the δ+ carbon in a haloalkane. Ammonia and bromoethane make ethylamine. But ethylamine has a lone pair too, so it attacks again. You get a mix of amines and even a salt with four groups on N. Use lots of ammonia to get mostly ethylamine.
adult: This is A-level organic chemistry (AQA 3.3.11, OCR A 6.2.1, Edexcel Topic 18). Students classify amines as primary, secondary or tertiary. They explain basicity with the nitrogen lone pair and write equations with acids. They describe making amines from haloalkanes and ammonia, including why mixtures form.

Basicity depends on how available the lone pair is to accept a proton. Alkyl groups have a positive inductive effect, so primary aliphatic amines are stronger bases than ammonia. In phenylamine the lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring, so it is a weaker base than ammonia. The pKa values of the conjugate acids are about 10.7, 9.3 and 4.6.

Common mistakes: classing amines by the carbon on the C–N carbon, as for alcohols, so (CH₃)₃CNH₂ is wrongly called tertiary. Students also write HBr instead of NH₄Br as the by-product. The balanced equation is CH₃CH₂Br + 2NH₃ → CH₃CH₂NH₂ + NH₄Br. Be careful not to claim tertiary amines are always strongest in water. Solvation of the ion also matters.

The reaction uses excess ethanolic ammonia heated in a sealed tube. Each amine formed is still a nucleophile, so further substitution gives secondary and tertiary amines and a quaternary ammonium salt. A large excess of ammonia favours the primary amine. Reducing a nitrile with LiAlH₄ gives the primary amine with no mixture. In the lab your teenager classifies amines, forms ammonium salts, ranks bases and controls the mixture with the mole ratio.

familyTip: Ask your teenager to explain, without notes, why heating bromoethane with ammonia gives more than one product, and what they would change to get mostly ethylamine.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: classify amines by carbons on N, protonate the lone pair, rank bases, control the bromoethane mixture and balance the equation.

practice.hint: Count only the carbons bonded directly to the nitrogen atom.
practice.explain: Only one carbon is bonded to N, so it is a primary amine. The three methyls are on that carbon, not on N.

practice.prompt: Using CH₃CH₂Br + 2NH₃ → CH₃CH₂NH₂ + NH₄Br, how many moles of ammonia are used up to make {n} mol of ethylamine?
practice.hint: Read the mole ratio of NH₃ to ethylamine from the balanced equation.
practice.explain: Two NH₃ react for each ethylamine, so {n} mol of ethylamine uses {=2*n} mol of ammonia.

practice.prompt: What forms when methylamine reacts with hydrochloric acid?
practice.hint: Which atom has a lone pair that can accept H⁺ from the acid?
practice.explain: The lone pair on N accepts H⁺, giving the methylammonium ion. With Cl⁻ this is the salt methylammonium chloride.

practice.prompt: Ethane-1,2-diamine, H₂NCH₂CH₂NH₂, has two NH₂ groups. How many moles of HCl react with {n} mol of it?
practice.hint: Each NH₂ group has one lone pair that can accept one H⁺.
practice.explain: Each molecule takes two H⁺, so {n} mol of the diamine reacts with {=2*n} mol of HCl.

pool.prompt: Which list is in order of increasing base strength?
pool.hint: Which lone pair is least available, and which is pushed out by an alkyl group?
pool.explain: In phenylamine the pair is delocalised into the ring, so it is weakest. The ethyl group's inductive effect makes ethylamine strongest.

pool.prompt: Why does ammonia with bromoethane give a mixture of amines?
choices: Ethylamine formed also has a lone pair and attacks bromoethane
Ammonia is a very weak nucleophile
pool.hint: Does the product still have a lone pair on nitrogen?
pool.explain: Each amine product is still a nucleophile, so it competes with ammonia. That gives secondary, tertiary and quaternary products.

pool.prompt: How can you make ethylamine the main product?
choices: Use a large excess of ammonia
Use a large excess of bromoethane
pool.hint: Which molecule should bromoethane usually bump into?
pool.explain: With excess ammonia, bromoethane nearly always meets NH₃, not ethylamine. Excess bromoethane pushes on to the quaternary salt.

pool.hint: Count every carbon group joined directly to the nitrogen atom.
pool.explain: N carries an ethyl and two methyl groups, so three carbons are bonded to it. It is tertiary, not quaternary, as it has no charge.

pool.prompt: Bromoethane reacts with {n} mol of ammonia until all of it becomes the quaternary salt (CH₃CH₂)₄N⁺ Br⁻. How many moles of bromoethane are needed?
pool.hint: Each ethyl group on N comes from one bromoethane.
pool.explain: Four ethyl groups end up on each N, so {n} mol of ammonia needs {=4*n} mol of bromoethane.

pool.prompt: What is the by-product in CH₃CH₂Br + 2NH₃ → CH₃CH₂NH₂ + ?
pool.hint: What happens to HBr when there is extra ammonia present?
pool.explain: Any HBr formed reacts with the second NH₃, so the by-product is ammonium bromide, NH₄Br.

pool.prompt: Ethylamine has Mr = 45. What mass in grams is {n} mol of ethylamine?
pool.hint: Mass equals moles multiplied by the relative molecular mass.

pool.prompt: Which route gives a primary amine with no mixture of products?
choices: Heat a haloalkane with a little ammonia
Mix ammonia and haloalkane in water at room temperature
pool.hint: Which route cannot add a second carbon group to nitrogen?
pool.explain: Nitrile reduction turns C≡N into CH₂NH₂ and nothing else, so no secondary or tertiary amines form.

pool.prompt: Why is the reaction of ammonia with a haloalkane done in a sealed tube?
choices: Ammonia is a gas and would escape on heating
pool.hint: What state is ammonia in at the reaction temperature?
pool.explain: Heating drives ammonia out of solution. A sealed tube keeps it in contact with the haloalkane.
